text: Here's the scenario. A new hire, Maria Chen, is starting Monday on a brand-new Facilities team. She'll work incidents assigned to her team, and eventually help build a few Facilities-specific catalog items. The director asks you, the administrator, to set all of that up. Let's walk through it exactly the way you'd actually handle this request on the job.

Step one: create her sys_user record, since Maria doesn't exist in the system yet. User_name matching your organization's convention, email filled in for notifications, active checked true since she starts Monday, and password_needs_reset checked so her temporary password gets replaced on first login. Right now she exists as a user, but with no role and no group, she can do almost nothing useful yet.

Step two: create the Facilities group in sys_user_group, since it doesn't exist yet either. Set the Group Email to the shared Facilities mailbox so notifications reach the whole growing team, and set Manager to the director. Step three: add Maria as a member from either form, writing one row to sys_user_grmember. Group membership alone still grants her zero permissions — that's not what groups are for.

Step four: decide on the role. Working incidents assigned to her team is baseline agent work, which maps directly to itil. You assign it, writing a row to sys_user_has_role. Before finalizing, you check what itil actually contains — confirming it sits low in the containment chain and doesn't implicitly grant anything beyond ordinary baseline agent access.

Step five is about restraint. The director mentioned future catalog work, which sounds like catalog_admin territory — but notice the word eventually. She isn't doing that work on day one, so granting it now would violate least privilege for no real benefit. The right move is to document the future need and grant catalog_admin only once that work actually begins — never jump straight to admin instead.

Step six: write the decision down. User created, group created, membership added, itil granted with containment verified, catalog_admin deliberately deferred, admin never considered. That one paragraph demonstrates every lesson in this chapter working together. Next up: Chapter 2 begins, and Lesson 6 asks how ACLs actually evaluate the access you just finished granting.
